crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines
children.blurb: Reproducible notebooks and pipelines cover the practice of making a quantitative analysis run again and produce the same result, whether on the original machine or another one months later.

children.name: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
children.blurb: Asking data questions in plain language covers the practice of putting a question to a dataset in ordinary words and getting back a result that can be checked, rather than writing SQL or a script by hand.

children.name: Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data
children.blurb: Large-scale compute on institutional data covers the practice of running heavy analytical workloads, such as model training, simulation, and statistical estimation, against datasets that an organisation holds under its own control rather than against public or scraped sources.

children.name: Writing Statistical Code with AI
children.blurb: Writing statistical code with AI covers the use of language models and code assistants to draft, refactor, and explain analysis scripts in languages such as R, Python, and Stata.

children.name: Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection
children.blurb: Testing a study design before data collection means checking that a planned analysis can actually answer the question it claims to answer, using simulated or pilot data rather than the real dataset.

sections.body: Quantitative analysis is the part of research where data becomes evidence, and artificial intelligence is now embedded in nearly every step of that path. In practice, models help write and debug analysis code, suggest statistical tests, translate plain-language questions into queries, and generate synthetic data for pilot runs. Notebooks and pipelines are being made reproducible with AI assistance that checks dependencies, flags hidden state, and reruns cells to confirm results. On institutional clusters, AI schedulers and code assistants help researchers use large compute allocations without hand-tuning every job. The work is less about replacing the analyst and more about shortening the loop between a question and a defensible answer.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are genuinely solved. Code completion for common statistical languages is reliable, and AI tools can now draft a working notebook from a clear specification. Reproducibility checks that compare outputs across runs are useful and increasingly automatic. What is not solved is correctness. A model can produce code that runs, looks plausible, and is statistically wrong, and it often cannot tell you which assumptions it has silently made. Plain-language querying works well on clean, well-documented tables and poorly on messy institutional data with inconsistent schemas. Large-scale compute assistance helps with mechanics but not with study design. The honest limit is that these tools accelerate execution while leaving judgment, validation, and interpretation with the researcher.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the arc of a study from setup to evidence. Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines is the foundation, covering how to keep an analysis rerunnable when AI writes or edits parts of it. Asking Data Questions in Plain Language sits at the front of the arc, for readers who want to turn a research question into a query without writing SQL or a dataframe script by hand. Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data addresses the middle, where the data is too big for a laptop and the work moves to shared clusters. Writing Statistical Code with AI is the craft page, focused on the specific failure modes of generated statistical code and how to test it. Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection closes the loop by using simulation and synthetic data to check whether a design can answer the question at all, before any real data is gathered.
